name: Essay Maps
description: Full essay architectures that capture how great essayists structure arguments

pg_discovery.name: PG Discovery
pg_discovery.description: Essay as thinking-out-loud. Starts with question, explores, discovers the question was wrong, finds better question, follows implications.
pg_discovery.source: Paul Graham essays (The Best Essay, How to Think for Yourself, etc.)

sections.name: QUESTION
sections.purpose: Open with genuine curiosity, not thesis
signals: My goal here is to figure out...
sections.requirement: Must be a real question you don't know the answer to yet
sections.substance_type: framing only - no evidence needed yet
sections.transition_to_next: End with the question clearly stated; next section answers it directly

sections.name: FIRST_ATTEMPT
sections.purpose: The obvious answer, explored honestly
signals: X, but you can Y about any Z. What makes it special is...
sections.requirement: Take the obvious answer seriously before rejecting it
sections.substance_type: Brief exploration, dismiss what's not interesting to find what is
sections.transition_to_next: State first conclusion in one simple sentence, then: 'That may sound obvious, but it has unexpected consequences'

cadence_archetypes: drumline - steady march through obvious options

sections.name: UNEXPECTED_CONSEQUENCE
sections.purpose: Following the obvious answer reveals something strange
signals: That may sound obvious, but it has some unexpected consequences.
sections.requirement: The strangeness must be genuinely surprising, not manufactured
substance_type: historical_example - proves point happened in real world
sections.transition_to_next: 'If [conclusion], then [implication]' OR 'I imagined X... But in fact the opposite seems true'

cadence_archetypes: crescendo_snap - build examples then land insight
ladder - each sentence builds on previous

sections.key_move: Use 'One is that... Another is...' to create list momentum

sections.name: WRONG_TURN_ACKNOWLEDGED
sections.purpose: Admit you were on the wrong track
signals: I imagined when I started... But in fact the opposite seems true
If that's true, then I started with the wrong question
sections.requirement: Genuine intellectual honesty - you changed your mind
substance_type: logical_reasoning - show why old view can't hold
sections.transition_to_next: 'Perhaps what this shows is...' OR 'Instead of asking X, I should have asked Y'

cadence_archetypes: long_short_snap - extended wrong view, then short correction

sections.name: BETTER_QUESTION
sections.purpose: Reframe to the real question
signals: Instead of asking X, I should have asked Y
There is, and on the face of it, it seems almost identical...
sections.requirement: New question must be earned by the previous exploration
sections.substance_type: distinction_explained - show how new question differs from old
sections.transition_to_next: State the new question, then: 'How do you do that?' OR ask reader's next question for them

sections.name: MECHANISM
sections.purpose: Explain WHY - the machinery underneath
sections.requirement: Not just what, but how and why it works that way
substance_type: process_description - step by step how it works
direct_instruction - 'You have to be very strict when...'
sections.transition_to_next: Ask the next natural question: 'Once you've got X, then what?' OR 'The most surprising question being thrown off at this point is...'

cadence_archetypes: wave - long explanation, short summary, long explanation

sections.length: 5-10 paragraphs - this is the heart of the essay

sections.name: IMPLICATIONS_FOLLOWED
sections.purpose: If this is true, what else must be true?
signals: This seems surprising enough to be worth investigating further
sections.requirement: Follow at least one surprising implication to its end
sections.transition_to_next: Can chain multiple implications with 'Another...' OR pivot to objection with 'It would be a mistake to let this...'

cadence_archetypes: parallel_march - similar structures for each implication

sections.length: 3-8 paragraphs depending on how many threads

sections.name: OBJECTION_ADDRESSED
sections.purpose: Steelman and answer the best counterargument
signals: It would be a mistake to...
sections.requirement: Real objection, not strawman
sections.transition_to_next: Resolve the objection, then return to main thread OR move to close

sections.name: CLOSE
sections.purpose: Return to start with new understanding
signals: So the answer to the original question...
This essay has been a kind of...
sections.requirement: Must connect back to opening, showing what was learned

transition_patterns.description: PG doesn't use transition words (Furthermore, However). He uses logical necessity.

types.name: logical_implication
types.pattern: If [conclusion from previous], then [what it means]
types.example: If the question reduces to making discoveries, then I started with the wrong question

types.name: reader_next_question
types.pattern: Ask what the reader is now thinking
types.example: Once you've got a question, then what?

types.name: list_momentum
types.pattern: 'One is that... Another is...' creates expectation
types.example: One is that science enters... Another unexpected consequence:

types.name: surprising_pivot
types.example: That may sound obvious, but it has some unexpected consequences

types.name: admission_pivot
types.pattern: 'I imagined X... But in fact Y'
types.example: I imagined when I started... But in fact the opposite seems to be true

types.name: answer_follows_question
types.pattern: Previous paragraph poses question, next answers it
types.example: P1 asks goal, P2 starts answering

anti_patterns: Furthermore / Moreover / Additionally
However (at start of paragraph)
In conclusion / To summarize
Firstly / Secondly / Thirdly (except in genuine lists)

substance_types.description: How to add depth and evidence at each point

types.name: historical_example
types.description: Proves the point happened in the real world
types.example: Darwin first described natural selection in an essay written in 1844

types.name: personal_admission
types.description: 'I don't... I just...' creates trust and specificity
types.example: I don't consciously rank branches this way; I just follow whichever seems most exciting

types.name: concrete_number
types.description: Specific beats vague
types.example: In this essay I've already cut a 17-paragraph subtree

types.name: mechanism_explained
types.description: HOW something works, not just that it does
types.example: Writing converts your ideas from vague to bad. But that's a step forward, because once you can see the brokenness, you can fix it.

types.name: mini_theory
types.description: Subcategorize to show depth of thinking
types.example: There are several ways to do that: [list of 4-5 approaches, each explained]

types.name: direct_instruction
types.description: 'You have to...' / 'The way to...'
types.example: You have to be very strict when rereading

types.name: rhetorical_question_as_test
types.description: Question that proves the point by being unanswerable or obvious
types.example: Talk about an important topic you could tell people something surprising about

pattern_library_integration.description: How to pull in sentence/paragraph patterns at each section

sentence_families: negation_pivot - it's not A, it's B

UNEXPECTED_CONSEQUENCE.use_heavily: This is where concrete examples land

MECHANISM.cadence: wave - long explanation, short summary, long explanation

key_principles: Show thinking, not thoughts - the reader watches you figure it out
Be willing to discover you were wrong
Each section earns the next - transitions are logical necessity, not bridges
Concrete examples at key moments as proof, not decoration
Follow surprising threads rather than staying on track
Meta-awareness without being annoying - you can reference the essay itself
MECHANISM section is the heart - spend the most time here
Substance comes from historical examples, personal admissions, concrete numbers, and mechanism explanations
failure_modes: Starting with conclusion disguised as question
Fake wrong turns (you knew the answer all along)
Sections that could be rearranged (not earned)
Assertions without mechanism
Ignoring the real objection
Using transition words instead of logical necessity
Light on MECHANISM section - that's where trust is built
No concrete examples - stays abstract
when_to_use: Genuinely exploring a question you don't know the answer to
Topics where the obvious answer is wrong or incomplete
Personal intellectual journey that others can learn from
When discovery IS the point - not just arriving at conclusion
Building trust through visible thinking process
When you want readers to change their minds alongside you

contrast_with_amodei_systematic.thesis: PG discovers thesis through writing; Amodei states thesis upfront
contrast_with_amodei_systematic.structure: PG follows implications organically; Amodei pre-plans categorical structure
contrast_with_amodei_systematic.reader_experience: PG: 'watch me figure it out'; Amodei: 'let me systematically convince you'
contrast_with_amodei_systematic.evidence: PG uses examples to illustrate; Amodei uses evidence to prove
contrast_with_amodei_systematic.tone: PG is intimate/personal; Amodei is authoritative/comprehensive
contrast_with_amodei_systematic.best_for: PG for intellectual exploration; Amodei for policy advocacy

amodei_systematic_analysis.name: Amodei Systematic Analysis
amodei_systematic_analysis.description: Essay as comprehensive risk/opportunity mapping. Opens with cultural framing, states thesis upfront, then systematically works through categories with consistent internal structure. Each category has analysis + defenses. Closes by returning to opening frame with call to action.
amodei_systematic_analysis.source: Dario Amodei essays (The Adolescence of Technology, Machines of Loving Grace)

sections.name: CULTURAL_FRAME
sections.purpose: Open with vivid scene from culture that embodies the stakes
sections.requirement: Must be recognizable cultural touchstone that captures emotional core
substance_type: emotional_stakes - what the scene makes us feel
sections.transition_to_next: Pivot from scene to thesis: 'This captures something real about...' OR 'The scene works because...'
sections.key_move: The scene must do double duty: emotionally engaging AND intellectually relevant

sections.name: THESIS_STATED
sections.purpose: Clearly state what you believe and what essay will argue
sections.requirement: Unlike PG discovery, thesis is known upfront - be direct
sections.transition_to_next: Announce the structure: 'There are [N] main categories...' OR 'I'll organize this around...'

sections.name: CATEGORICAL_OVERVIEW
sections.purpose: Preview the categories you'll analyze
sections.requirement: Categories must be MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) or explain why not
sections.substance_type: category_names - just the labels, save depth for later
sections.transition_to_next: Transition to first category: 'Let's start with...' OR simply begin first section

cadence_archetypes: parallel_march - consistent structure for each preview

sections.name: CATEGORY_SECTION
sections.purpose: Deep dive into one category with consistent internal structure

internal_structure.name: CATEGORY_HEADER
signals: Section title plus subtitle or quote
internal_structure.requirement: Title should be memorable - mix technical and cultural reference

internal_structure.name: PROBLEM_STATEMENT
internal_structure.purpose: State what the risk/concern actually is
substance_type: concrete_scenario - specific example of risk manifesting
mechanism_explained - how the risk actually works
spectrum_laid_out - show range from mild to severe

internal_structure.name: DETAILED_ANALYSIS
internal_structure.purpose: Work through nuances, sub-cases, real-world implications
substance_type: probability_assessment - how likely is each variant?

internal_structure.name: DEFENSES
internal_structure.purpose: What can be done to mitigate this category of risk
signals: Several factors work in our favor...
internal_structure.requirement: Must be concrete and actionable, not hand-wavy

sections.transition_to_next: Can be minimal - section headers do heavy lifting. Or: 'Moving to the next category...'
sections.length: 10-30 paragraphs per category depending on complexity

sections.name: SYNTHESIS
sections.purpose: What do the categories together reveal?
sections.requirement: Must add insight beyond sum of parts
substance_type: priority_argued - which matters most and why
sections.transition_to_next: Pivot to action: 'Given all this, what should we do?' OR return to opening frame

sections.name: RETURN_TO_FRAME
sections.purpose: Callback to opening scene with new understanding
sections.requirement: Must show how analysis has deepened understanding of opening
sections.transition_to_next: Flow into call to action

sections.name: CALL_TO_ACTION
sections.purpose: Issue challenge to reader/society
sections.requirement: Must feel earned by the analysis - not generic uplift
substance_type: stakes_restated - what hangs in the balance?

transition_patterns.description: Amodei uses explicit structure (numbered sections, headers) plus clear signposting

types.name: section_header
types.pattern: Numbered section with title in quotes or parenthetical
types.example: 2. Misuse for destruction ("A surprising and terrible empowerment")

types.name: defenses_pivot
types.pattern: Shift from problem to solution with single word header
types.example: Defenses:

types.name: explicit_signpost
types.example: I'll organize my thoughts around five main buckets...

types.name: scope_acknowledgment
types.pattern: Note what you're not covering and why
types.example: I won't discuss X in depth here, but it deserves mention...

types.name: frame_callback
types.example: Return to the scene I opened with...

anti_patterns: Transitions that work against explicit structure
Surprise pivots in a systematic essay
Burying category boundaries

substance_types.description: Amodei essays are evidence-heavy with policy focus

types.name: footnoted_evidence
types.description: Citation-supported claims with sources
types.example: The nuclear taboo has held for 80 years [footnote with sources]

types.name: concrete_scenario
types.description: Specific hypothetical that makes abstract risk concrete
types.example: Imagine a model that can synthesize a pathogen from openly available research...

types.name: spectrum_analysis
types.description: Show range from mild to severe versions
types.example: At the mild end... at the severe end...

types.name: policy_proposal
types.description: Specific actionable intervention
types.example: Requiring KYC for frontier model access...

types.name: honest_limitation
types.description: Acknowledge where your defenses are weak
types.example: None of these defenses are perfect. The concern remains that...

types.name: probability_estimate
types.description: Explicit likelihood assessment
types.example: I'd estimate a 10-20% chance that... a smaller but non-negligible chance that...

types.name: historical_analogy
types.description: Previous technology/situation that parallels current one
types.example: The nuclear era offers lessons... The early days of the internet show...
types.when_to_use: Any section - ground abstract in concrete precedent

types.name: cultural_reference
types.description: Movie, book, artwork that captures the concern
types.example: HAL 9000... Skynet... Player Piano...

pattern_library_integration.description: How to pull in sentence/paragraph patterns at each section

sentence_families: conditional_snap - if X then Y consequences

key_principles: Thesis upfront - this is advocacy, not exploration
Systematic coverage - MECE categories or explain why not
Consistent internal structure - each category follows same pattern
Evidence-heavy - footnotes, citations, specific numbers
Honest about limitations - acknowledge where defenses are weak
Cultural framing - use recognizable references to set stakes
Action-oriented close - don't just analyze, call for action
Balance doom and hope - risks are real but defenses exist
failure_modes: Categories that overlap or leave gaps
Defenses section that's generic or hand-wavy
Opening frame that doesn't connect to analysis
Call to action that feels unearned
All doom, no defenses (or vice versa)
Abstract risks without concrete scenarios
Missing the synthesis - just listing categories
Closing that doesn't return to opening frame
when_to_use: Complex multi-faceted topic requiring systematic treatment
Risk or opportunity analysis
Policy-oriented writing
When you have a thesis to argue (not discover)
Topics where categorization helps understanding
When you need to be comprehensive, not just insightful

contrast_with_pg_discovery.thesis: PG discovers thesis through writing; Amodei states thesis upfront
contrast_with_pg_discovery.structure: PG follows implications organically; Amodei pre-plans categorical structure
contrast_with_pg_discovery.reader_experience: PG: 'watch me figure it out'; Amodei: 'let me systematically convince you'
contrast_with_pg_discovery.evidence: PG uses examples to illustrate; Amodei uses evidence to prove
contrast_with_pg_discovery.tone: PG is intimate/personal; Amodei is authoritative/comprehensive
contrast_with_pg_discovery.best_for: PG for intellectual exploration; Amodei for policy advocacy

pg_analogy_exploration.name: PG Analogy Exploration
pg_analogy_exploration.description: Essay built around a surprising comparison between two domains. Opens with observation that two things seem unrelated, reveals deep structural similarities, follows implications. Reader discovers that understanding one domain illuminates the other.
pg_analogy_exploration.source: Paul Graham essays (Hackers and Painters, Beating the Averages)

sections.name: SURPRISING_PAIRING
sections.purpose: Establish that you've moved between two worlds others see as unrelated
signals: When I finished X, I went to Y...
A lot of people seemed surprised that...
They seemed to think X and Y were very different...
sections.requirement: Personal credibility in both domains; the pairing must seem genuinely unexpected
sections.substance_type: personal_credential - establish you know both worlds
sections.transition_to_next: State that conventional view is wrong: 'Both of these images are wrong.'

sections.name: CORE_SIMILARITY
sections.purpose: Name the deep structural similarity between the domains
signals: What X and Y have in common is...
sections.requirement: The similarity must be non-obvious but, once stated, feel true
substance_type: category_definition - what class do both belong to?
shared_property - what do they both do?
sections.transition_to_next: Having established similarity, complicate it: 'I've never liked the term...'

sections.name: CONVENTIONAL_FRAME_CRITIQUE
sections.purpose: Show how the standard framing of one domain is broken
signals: The main reason I don't like it is...
X is a grab bag of...
At one end... in the middle... at the other extreme...
sections.requirement: Must show that conventional categories obscure rather than illuminate
substance_type: taxonomy_exposed - show the mess of current categories
concrete_examples - specific cases that don't fit
historical_accident - why things are the way they are
sections.transition_to_next: Propose the better frame: 'Perhaps one day...' OR 'The other reason I don't like...'

sections.name: LESSONS_FROM_ANALOGY
sections.purpose: Draw specific insights from comparing the two domains
signals: What can X teach us about Y?
For example, I was taught in college that...
sections.requirement: Insights must be concrete and actionable, not just 'they're similar'
substance_type: personal_anecdote - how you learned this lesson
counterintuitive_practice - what the analogy reveals you should do
wrong_approach_exposed - what happens when you don't follow it
sections.transition_to_next: Can chain multiple lessons with 'Another example...' OR pivot to objection

cadence_archetypes: wave - long example, short lesson, long example

sections.length: 8-15 paragraphs - this is the bulk of the essay

sections.name: INSTITUTIONAL_FAILURE
sections.purpose: Show how institutions get the domains wrong
sections.requirement: Must identify specific institutional forces that create the problem
substance_type: personal_experience - your encounter with the institution
structural_analysis - why the failure is systematic
sections.transition_to_next: Move to solution or opportunity: 'So one way to...' OR 'The place to...'

sections.name: WAY_FORWARD
sections.purpose: What to do given these insights
signals: This is what X is all about...
sections.requirement: Must be practical, not just theoretical
substance_type: reframing - how to see your situation differently
sections.transition_to_next: Can add complications or move to close

sections.name: CLOSE_WITH_STAKES
sections.purpose: Why this matters beyond the practical
signals: What we can say with some confidence is...
Over and over we see the same pattern...
How cool X turns out to be will depend on...
sections.requirement: Must elevate from practical to significant without grandiosity
substance_type: open_question - what remains to be seen

transition_patterns.description: PG Analogy uses the analogy itself as transition infrastructure

types.name: domain_switch
types.pattern: Move from one domain to the other
types.example: Because painters leave a trail of work behind them...

types.name: lesson_extraction
types.example: Here's a case where we can learn from painting.

types.name: personal_discovery
types.pattern: Use your own realization as bridge
types.example: Now I realize I was mistaken.

types.name: institutional_pivot
types.pattern: Move from insight to systemic problem
types.example: If universities and research labs keep hackers from doing...

anti_patterns: Forced analogies that don't hold up
Staying too long in one domain
Making the comparison but not extracting lessons

substance_types.description: Analogy essays thrive on concrete details from both domains

types.name: cross_domain_example
types.description: Show same pattern in both domains
types.example: Paintings usually begin with a sketch... I think hacking should work this way too.
types.when_to_use: LESSONS_FROM_ANALOGY - prove the similarity is real

types.name: personal_wrong_turn
types.description: Admit you used to believe the wrong thing
types.example: For a long time I felt bad about this, just as I once felt bad that I didn't hold my pencil the way they taught me.

types.name: institutional_quote
types.description: Let institutions indict themselves
types.example: Programs should be written for people to read, and only incidentally for machines to execute.

types.name: maker_solidarity
types.description: Reference other makers who share the pattern
types.example: Benjamin Franklin learned to write by summarizing... Raymond Chandler did the same thing...

key_principles: The analogy must reveal, not just compare
Both domains must be treated with equal respect and knowledge
Personal experience in both domains builds credibility
Lessons must be concrete and actionable
Institutional critique gives the essay stakes
The reader should see their own domain differently by the end
failure_modes: Analogy that's cute but doesn't hold up under pressure
Too abstract - no concrete details from either domain
One-sided - expert in one domain, tourist in the other
No lessons extracted - just 'they're similar!'
No institutional critique - stays at individual level
Preaching - the reader feels lectured, not enlightened
when_to_use: You have genuine experience in two domains others see as unrelated
You've noticed structural similarities others miss
The comparison yields actionable insights
There's an institutional failure to critique
You want to reframe how people see a field

raymond_case_study.name: Raymond Case Study
raymond_case_study.description: Essay built around a first-person case study that extracts numbered principles. Tells the story of a project while explicitly pulling out lessons as numbered aphorisms. Reader learns both the story and a reusable framework.
raymond_case_study.source: Eric S. Raymond (The Cathedral and the Bazaar, Homesteading the Noosphere)

sections.name: PARADIGM_CHALLENGE
sections.purpose: State that conventional wisdom about something is wrong
sections.requirement: Must name the surprising phenomenon that challenges the paradigm
sections.transition_to_next: Establish your credibility: 'By the time X swam onto my radar screen...'

sections.name: PERSONAL_CREDENTIAL
sections.purpose: Establish why you're qualified to analyze this
signals: I had already been involved in X for Y years...
I was one of the first...
I thought I knew how it was done.
sections.requirement: Must show both expertise AND that you were surprised
substance_type: prior_beliefs - what you thought you knew
sections.transition_to_next: Name what overturned your assumptions: 'X overturned much of what I thought I knew.'

sections.name: CENTRAL_METAPHOR
sections.purpose: Introduce the framing metaphor for the essay
signals: I believed that... needed to be built like cathedrals...
The X community seemed to resemble...
sections.requirement: Metaphor must be vivid, memorable, and actually illuminate
sections.transition_to_next: Signal the essay's method: 'Chance handed me a perfect way to test my theory...'

sections.name: CASE_STUDY_NARRATIVE
sections.purpose: Tell the story of your project with embedded lessons
signals: This is the story of that project.
I'll use it to propose some aphorisms...
sections.requirement: Story must be specific enough to be credible, general enough to yield principles

internal_structure.name: STORY_BEAT
internal_structure.purpose: A specific event or decision in the project

internal_structure.name: LESSON_EXTRACTION
internal_structure.purpose: Pull out a numbered principle from the beat
internal_structure.requirement: Principle must be memorable and reusable

sections.transition_to_next: Story naturally leads to theory: 'By mid-1996 I thought I was beginning to understand.'

cadence_archetypes: wave - story beat, lesson, story beat, lesson

sections.name: THEORETICAL_FRAMEWORK
sections.purpose: Generalize from case study to theory
signals: Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow.
sections.requirement: Theory must emerge from story, not be imposed on it
substance_type: named_law - give your principle a name
sections.transition_to_next: Address objections or expand scope

sections.name: BROADER_IMPLICATIONS
sections.purpose: What does this mean beyond your case study?
signals: If I'm correct, they'll help you...
The implications for the future of...
This insight can be extended to...
sections.requirement: Must be intellectually ambitious without losing grounding
substance_type: scope_expansion - where else does this apply?
prediction - what will happen if this is right?

transition_patterns.description: Raymond uses numbered lessons as structural spine

types.name: lesson_marker
types.example: 5. When you lose interest in a program, your last duty to it is to hand it off to a competent successor.

types.name: story_continuation
types.example: The next thing I needed was...

types.name: theoretical_pivot
types.example: This suggested a deeper point...

types.name: scope_expansion
types.example: If this is true for software, what about...?

anti_patterns: Lessons that feel forced or obvious
Story that wanders without extracting lessons
Theory disconnected from story
Too many lessons (diminishing returns)

key_principles: The story must be real and specific
Lessons must be numbered and memorable
Theory must emerge from story, not precede it
The metaphor does heavy organizational work
Personal credibility matters - you must have done the thing
The lessons should be reusable by others
failure_modes: Lessons that are obvious or trite
Story without generalizable lessons
Theory disconnected from evidence
Metaphor that doesn't hold up
Too much technical detail for general audience
Not enough technical detail for credibility
when_to_use: You've done a project that yielded surprising insights
You want to teach through story rather than abstract principles
The lessons are genuinely novel and reusable
You have a good central metaphor
You want readers to apply your insights to their own work

stephenson_cultural_excavation.name: Stephenson Cultural Excavation
stephenson_cultural_excavation.description: Essay as archaeological dig through culture. Uses technology as lens to examine deeper questions about society, consciousness, and meaning. Long, digressive, rich with extended metaphors and historical context. Reader emerges with new way of seeing familiar things.
stephenson_cultural_excavation.source: Neal Stephenson (In the Beginning was the Command Line, The Great Simoleon Caper)

sections.name: HISTORICAL_FRAMING
sections.purpose: Ground the topic in specific historical moment
sections.requirement: Must establish specific actors, dates, and context
substance_type: named_actors - specific people who made decisions
weird_detail - thing that now seems strange
sections.transition_to_next: Pivot to present implications: 'A person who went into a coma before... and woke up now...'

sections.name: EXTENDED_METAPHOR_SETUP
sections.purpose: Introduce the controlling metaphor for the essay
signals: The analogy between X and Y is not half bad...
Let me run with it for a moment...
sections.requirement: Metaphor must be elaborated in loving detail, not just named
substance_type: vivid_detail - make the metaphor world real
sections.transition_to_next: Apply metaphor to current situation

sections.name: CULTURAL_ARCHAEOLOGY
sections.purpose: Dig through layers of cultural meaning
signals: What the hell is going on here?
This is not such a bad thing in...
The metaphor shear was especially brutal...
sections.requirement: Must uncover assumptions people don't know they're making
substance_type: hidden_assumption_exposed - what everyone takes for granted
class_analysis - who benefits from current arrangement
personal_anecdote - your encounter with the phenomenon
sections.transition_to_next: Sections can chain through multiple aspects of the phenomenon
sections.length: 20-40 paragraphs - this is where the essay lives

sections.name: PHILOSOPHICAL_DIGRESSION
sections.purpose: Step back to larger questions about meaning and society
signals: The word, in the end, is the only system of encoding thoughts...
We want things to be easier...
This is precisely the same as...
sections.requirement: Must connect specific phenomenon to universal human concerns
substance_type: universal_claim - what this says about humans
self_implication - the author is part of this too
sections.transition_to_next: Return to specific with new understanding

sections.name: RESOLUTION_OR_IMPASSE
sections.purpose: Where does this leave us?
signals: In the end, there's just a fundamental tension...
sections.requirement: Must be honest about what remains unresolved

transition_patterns.description: Stephenson uses associative flow rather than strict logic

types.name: cultural_riff
types.example: This reminds one of... Speaking of which...

types.name: technical_to_cultural
types.pattern: Move from technical detail to cultural meaning
types.example: This is not just a technical matter. It reflects...

types.name: personal_intrusion
types.example: I myself had an experience that...

types.name: digression_acknowledged
types.example: (Note: many readers... rest assured that I am actually positioning my pieces on the chessboard...)

anti_patterns: Digressions that never return
Cultural analysis without specific examples
Preaching without self-implication
Metaphors that collapse under pressure

substance_types.description: Stephenson uses cultural artifacts as primary evidence

types.name: cultural_artifact
types.description: Specific movie, book, product, or event as evidence
types.example: When Ronald Reagan was a radio announcer, he used to call baseball games by reading the terse descriptions that trickled in over the telegraph wire...

types.name: personal_memory
types.description: Specific autobiographical episode
types.example: In order to connect this device (which was not a computer at all) to the Iowa State University mainframe across town...

types.name: class_observation
types.description: Who benefits from the current arrangement
types.example: Morlocks, who have the energy and intelligence to comprehend details, go out and master complex subjects...

types.name: metaphor_extension
types.description: Push the controlling metaphor further
types.example: On the other side of the road are two competitors that have come along more recently...

key_principles: Technology is lens for culture, not the subject itself
Digressions are features, not bugs - but must return
Extended metaphors must be elaborated in loving detail
Self-awareness and humor prevent preachiness
Historical grounding prevents abstraction
The author must be implicated in the analysis
failure_modes: Digressions that don't illuminate
Preaching without self-implication
Metaphors that can't sustain weight
Cultural analysis without historical grounding
Too clever - prioritizing wit over insight
Too long without payoff
when_to_use: Technology reveals something about human nature
You have an extended metaphor that truly illuminates
The topic requires historical and cultural context
You're willing to digress and trust the reader to follow
There's no clean resolution - just clearer seeing
example_essays: In the Beginning was the Command Line (1999)

wolfram_explanatory_build.name: Wolfram Explanatory Build
wolfram_explanatory_build.description: Essay as systematic explanation building from simple to complex. Opens with 'how does X work?' and proceeds through layers of increasing detail. Heavy use of examples, diagrams, and interactive elements. Reader builds understanding layer by layer.
wolfram_explanatory_build.source: Stephen Wolfram (What Is ChatGPT Doing, A New Kind of Science essays)

sections.name: CORE_QUESTION
sections.purpose: Ask the fundamental 'how does X work?' question
signals: My purpose here is to give a rough outline of...
The first thing to explain is...
sections.requirement: Question must be genuine - something readers want answered
sections.substance_type: question_framed - what we're trying to understand
sections.transition_to_next: Begin answering immediately: 'The first thing to explain is...'

sections.name: SIMPLEST_VERSION
sections.purpose: Explain the basic mechanism in its simplest form
signals: At some level it's quite simple...
What X is always fundamentally trying to do is...
sections.requirement: Must be genuinely simple - the foundation for everything else
sections.transition_to_next: Complicate with specifics: 'But, OK, at each step...'

sections.name: WORKED_EXAMPLE
sections.purpose: Show the mechanism in action with specific case
sections.requirement: Example must be concrete enough to follow, simple enough to understand
substance_type: variations - what happens if you change things
sections.transition_to_next: Ask the next question: 'So where do the X come from?'

sections.name: UNDERLYING_MECHANISM
sections.purpose: Go one level deeper - what's underneath the surface?
signals: OK, so where do the X come from?
Let's start with a simpler problem...
The key is the notion of...
sections.requirement: Must connect surface behavior to deeper structure
substance_type: simplified_model - easier version of the problem
sections.transition_to_next: Add the next layer: 'But this is where a key idea comes in...'

sections.name: KEY_INSIGHT
sections.purpose: Name the crucial conceptual leap
sections.requirement: Must be a genuine insight, not just restating the mechanism
substance_type: concept_named - give the insight a name
sections.transition_to_next: Apply insight or address complications

sections.name: COMPLICATIONS
sections.purpose: Address what makes this harder than it first seemed
signals: In practice, it turns out that...
sections.requirement: Must deepen understanding, not just add caveats
substance_type: limits_acknowledged - what we still don't know
sections.transition_to_next: Move to synthesis or broader implications

sections.name: SYNTHESIS_AND_SIGNIFICANCE
sections.purpose: What have we learned and why does it matter?
signals: So what is X really doing?
And the remarkable thing is that...
sections.requirement: Must connect back to opening question and go beyond
substance_type: scientific_significance - what this tells us about the world

transition_patterns.description: Wolfram uses explicit question-answer as spine

types.name: question_posed
types.pattern: Ask what reader is now wondering
types.example: OK, so where do those probabilities come from?

types.name: simplification
types.example: Let's start with a simpler problem.

types.name: complication
types.example: But in practice, things are more complicated.

types.name: level_change
types.example: What's going on underneath all this?

anti_patterns: Jumping to complexity before establishing basics
Too many levels without concrete examples
Losing the thread of what question we're answering
Technical jargon without explanation

substance_types.description: Wolfram uses visual examples as primary evidence

types.name: computed_example
types.description: Actually run the thing and show results
types.example: [image of neural net output]

types.name: simplified_model
types.description: Toy version that shows core mechanism
types.example: Consider a 'language' formed from sequences of ('s and )'s...

types.name: historical_context
types.description: How we got to current understanding
types.example: Invented—in a form remarkably close to their use today—in the 1940s...

types.name: code_snippet
types.description: Actual runnable code
types.example: [Wolfram Language code]

key_principles: Start simple, add complexity layer by layer
Always ground in concrete examples
Ask the reader's questions before they do
Show don't just tell - use visuals
Be honest about what's not understood
Connect to larger scientific significance
failure_modes: Starting too complex
Too much abstraction without examples
Jargon without explanation
Losing the thread of the central question
Examples that are too simplified to be useful
Missing the 'so what?' - why does this matter
when_to_use: Explaining how a complex system works
Topic can be understood through progressive complexity
You can show concrete examples of the mechanism
Reader genuinely wants to understand, not just know
The explanation yields genuine insights
example_essays: What Is ChatGPT Doing … and Why Does It Work? (2023)
The Empirical Metamathematics of Euclid and Beyond (2020)
A New Kind of Science (2002) - core chapters
